title: Design a chain of consensus system
evidence: One 2026 GovTech SWE interview account (a Glassdoor search snippet, unverified) names this one-line prompt, in the same process as the Roving on Mars live-coding round; no further spec was reported.
prompt:
"Design a chain of consensus system."

That is the whole prompt. The interviewer stays quiet to see how you turn one vague line into a system you can defend.

clarify.q: Can a node lie, or do nodes only crash?
clarify.a: Assume the nodes are run by agencies we trust, so crashes are the main risk. Tell me what changes if one node is compromised.

clarify.q: Who are the participants? Anyone, or a known set?
clarify.a: A known set: 5 to 7 agency nodes. Nobody joins without approval.

clarify.q: What throughput and commit latency do you need?
clarify.a: Up to 2,000 transactions a second at peak. Commit within a second is fine.
Opaque records: audit events, certificate issuance. No balances or smart contracts.
One region, several availability zones. A second region is a stretch goal.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.ask: Turn "chain" and "consensus" into concrete functional and non-functional requirements. Say your interpretation out loud.
steps.model:
Interpretation: a permissioned, replicated, append-only ledger. "Consensus" means every healthy node holds the same transactions in the same order. "Chain" means blocks linked by hashes so tampering shows.

  • Functional: submit a transaction and get a receipt; read a transaction with its block height and an inclusion proof; read blocks by height; verify the chain from genesis.
  • Non-functional: survive 2 crashed nodes; commit in under 1 s; never lose an acknowledged write (fsync on a majority before the ack); tamper-evident history; reads can be slightly stale unless the caller asks for fresh.
  • Out of scope: open membership, mining, tokens, smart contracts.

Say: "I'll design for crash faults with Raft, then show what changes for Byzantine faults."

steps.title: Estimates
steps.ask: Size the write rate, network, block size and storage growth. What do the numbers tell you?
steps.model:
• Peak 2,000 tx/s × 1 KB = 2 MB/s into the leader.
  • The leader sends each entry to 4 followers: ~8 MB/s (64 Mbps) out. One NIC handles that easily.
  • Blocks sealed every 200 ms: 2,000 × 0.2 = 400 tx, ~400 KB per block.
  • Average 200 tx/s × 1 KB × 86,400 × 365 = ~6.3 TB a year per node.
  • Commit latency in one region: one round trip to the 2 fastest followers (~1 ms) + fsync (~2 ms) + batch wait: ~5-10 ms.

Conclusion: a single leader is not the bottleneck at this rate. Storage growth is the long-run cost, so plan snapshots and archiving from day one.

steps.title: API & data model
steps.ask: Define the API and what each node stores.
steps.model:
• POST /tx {payload, clientId, nonce, signature} → 202 {txId}. (clientId, nonce) is the idempotency key, so a retried submit is not appended twice.
  • GET /tx/{id} → {status, height, index, merkleProof}.
  • GET /blocks/{height}, GET /verify?from=.

Per node, on local disk (RocksDB or files):

  • Raft log: (term, index, tx), fsynced.
  • Blocks: height, prev_hash, merkle_root, timestamp, leader_sig, tx_ids[].
  • Tx index: txId → (height, position) plus the dedupe set of recent nonces.
  • Snapshots of the index so a new node does not replay years of log.

steps.title: High-level design
steps.ask: Draw the components and walk one write from client to committed block.
steps.model:
Five ledger nodes spread 2-2-1 over three availability zones, behind a load balancer.

  1. Client sends POST /tx to any node. A follower forwards it to the leader.
  2. The leader checks the signature and dedupe set, then appends to its Raft log, batching entries that arrive within a few milliseconds.
  3. It sends AppendEntries to all followers. Each writes to disk, fsyncs and replies.
  4. Once 3 of 5 have the entry on disk it is committed. The leader replies to the client.
  5. Every node applies committed entries in log order: the sealer builds a block with the previous block's hash and a Merkle root of the transactions, so all nodes produce identical blocks.

Reads go to the leader (with a lease) when fresh data is required, or to any follower otherwise. Metrics: commit latency, follower lag, election count.

steps.title: Deep dive
steps.ask: Go deep on one part. Suggested: how leader failure is handled safely, and what Byzantine faults would change.
steps.model:
Leader failure. Followers expect heartbeats every ~50 ms. If none arrive within a randomised 150-300 ms timeout, a follower becomes a candidate, increments the term and asks for votes. A node votes only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own, so a new leader always holds every committed entry. Any two majorities of 5 overlap in at least one node, so two leaders cannot win the same term, and a deposed leader cannot get a majority to commit.

With 2 nodes down, 3 remain: writes continue. With 3 down, writes stop. That is a deliberate CP choice: no split-brain ledger.

Byzantine faults. If a node may lie, use PBFT or Tendermint: 3f+1 = 7 nodes for f = 2, every vote signed, a block commits after 2f+1 matching signatures. Messages grow as n², so keep membership small.

steps.title: Bottlenecks & trade-offs
steps.ask: Name the bottlenecks and the trade-offs you made.
steps.model:
• Leader throughput: batch entries and pipeline AppendEntries. Beyond ~20k tx/s, shard into several independent chains by agency or record type.
  • fsync cost: group commit and NVMe disks. Skipping fsync breaks the durability promise.
  • Ledger growth (~6 TB/year): snapshot the index, move old blocks to object storage, keep their hashes so verification still works.
  • Multi-region: a majority must answer, so commit latency rises from ~5 ms to ~30-60 ms. Worth it only if a region loss must not stop writes.
  • Raft vs BFT: Raft is simpler and faster but trusts nodes. BFT costs 2 extra nodes and more messages.
  • Why not a public blockchain: unknown participants are not a requirement, and probabilistic finality and fees buy nothing here.

rubric: Asks whether faults are crash-only or Byzantine before choosing a protocol.
States the commit rule: an entry is acknowledged only after a majority (3 of 5) has it on disk.
Explains hash-linking (prev_hash) and how it makes tampering detectable.
Gives node counts from fault tolerance: 2f+1 for crash, 3f+1 for Byzantine.
Makes submits idempotent so a retry is not appended twice.
Explains leader election and why two leaders cannot both commit.
Says what happens when a majority is lost (writes stop) and calls it a CP choice.
Plans for ledger growth with snapshots or archiving.

title: Design a rate limiter API
evidence: An anonymous GovTech interview listing on NodeFlair (a search snippet, unverified) names this prompt; it is also a standard industry question.
prompt: "Design a rate limiter API. Our public APIs and login endpoints sit behind several gateway instances. We want to cap how often each caller can hit them."

clarify.q: Limit by what: user, IP, API key, endpoint?
clarify.a: Per API key for the data APIs. Per IP and per phone number for the OTP endpoints.
Hard. Blocked callers get an error they can act on.
About 50k requests a second at peak across 20 gateway instances.
One region for now.

clarify.q: Must rules change without a deploy?
clarify.a: Yes. Ops should be able to tighten a limit during an incident.

clarify.q: What if the limiter itself is down?
clarify.a: Your call. Justify it.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.ask: List what the limiter must do and the qualities it must have.
steps.model:
• Functional: decide allow or deny per request for a key (API key, IP, phone) and a rule (e.g. 100 req/min per key, 5 OTP requests per phone per hour); return remaining quota; let ops create and change rules at runtime; blocked callers get 429 with Retry-After.
  • Non-functional: adds about 1 ms; correct across 20 gateways (one shared count, not 20 separate ones); highly available; allows short bursts; memory bounded.
  • Out of scope: billing, DDoS at the network layer (that is the CDN/WAF's job), global multi-region quotas.

Note the two use cases differ: data APIs care about fairness, OTP endpoints care about abuse and SMS cost. That will matter for failure handling.

steps.title: Estimates
steps.ask: Estimate request rate, store operations, memory and latency.
steps.model:
• Peak 50k req/s, one limiter check each: 50k Redis script calls/s.
  • One Redis shard handles ~25k Lua calls/s with headroom, so 2 shards, run 3.
  • 10M active keys × ~100 B (key + tokens + timestamp + overhead) = ~1 GB for token buckets.
  • A sliding log keeping 100 timestamps per key would be 10M × 100 × 8 B = ~8 GB. This is why we avoid it.
  • 1,000 rules × 200 B = 200 KB: every gateway can cache all rules in memory.
  • One in-zone Redis round trip: ~0.5-1 ms added latency.

Conclusion: a small Redis cluster is enough. The design is about correctness and failure modes, not raw scale.

steps.title: API & data model
steps.ask: Define the check API, the admin API, the response contract and the stored state.
steps.model:
• Check (in-process library or sidecar call): check(key, ruleId, cost=1) → {allowed, remaining, resetAt, retryAfter}.
  • Admin: PUT /v1/rules/{id} {match, limit, windowSec, burst, failMode}, GET /v1/rules.
  • Response headers on every call: RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset; on block: 429 + Retry-After.

State:

  • Redis hash rl:{ruleId}:{key} → tokens, lastRefillMs, TTL = 2 × window so idle keys disappear.
  • Postgres rules table as the source of truth; gateways cache it and refresh on a pub/sub message or every 30 s.

In Redis Cluster one script may only touch keys in one hash slot, so run one script per bucket, or give buckets checked together a shared hash tag such as {apiKey}.

steps.title: High-level design
steps.ask: Draw the request path and the rules path.
steps.model:
1. Client → load balancer → one of 20 gateway instances.
  2. Gateway middleware matches the request to rules from its in-memory cache (API key rule, IP rule, phone rule).
  3. It calls Redis with one Lua script per matching bucket, pipelined in a single round trip; each script checks and updates its bucket atomically.
  4. Allowed: forward to the upstream service with rate-limit headers. Denied: return 429 immediately; the upstream never sees it.
  5. Every decision increments a metric; a dashboard shows 429 rate per rule and top blocked keys.

Rules path: ops edits a rule in the admin UI → rules service writes Postgres → publishes "rules changed" → gateways reload within seconds. No deploy needed.

Enforce at the gateway so every service gets it for free; services can still add finer limits inside.

steps.title: Deep dive
steps.ask: Go deep on the algorithm and how it stays correct with many gateways.
steps.model:
Token bucket: capacity B, refill rate r per second. On each request: tokens = min(B, tokens + (now - last) × r); if tokens ≥ cost, subtract and allow, else deny. It allows bursts up to B and an average of r.

Atomic: read-modify-write from 20 gateways would race and let extra requests through. Redis runs a Lua script to completion before the next command, so the whole check is atomic. Use Redis TIME inside the script so gateway clock skew does not matter.

Alternatives: fixed window counters are simplest but allow 2× the limit across a window boundary. A sliding log is exact but costs ~8 GB here. A sliding window counter (current count + previous count × overlap) is a close approximation at two integers per key, a good choice when bursts must not exceed the limit.

steps.title: Bottlenecks & trade-offs
steps.ask: What breaks first, and what did you trade?
steps.model:
• Redis down: decide per rule. Data APIs fail open (availability matters more than exact quotas). OTP endpoints fail closed or fall back to a coarse in-memory limit per gateway, because an open OTP endpoint costs money and enables brute force.
  • Latency: if 1 ms is too much, each gateway can take 10 tokens at a time and spend them locally. Faster, but the limit is less exact.
  • Hot keys: one big agency key at 5k req/s lands on one shard. Local pre-limiting absorbs most of it.
  • Shared IPs: a whole office or mobile carrier NAT can share one IP. Limit by API key or user where possible, and keep IP limits generous.
  • Multi-region: split the budget per region rather than synchronising counts across regions.

rubric: Clarifies what the limit is keyed on (user, IP, API key, phone) before designing.
Names an algorithm (token bucket or sliding window) and explains its burst behaviour.
Uses a shared store with an atomic check (Lua script or equivalent) so gateways do not race.
Returns 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers.
Sizes memory and store throughput with real numbers.
Chooses fail open or fail closed deliberately, and differently for login/OTP versus data APIs.
Lets rules change at runtime without a deploy.
Mentions hot keys or shared IPs (NAT) as a practical problem.

title: Multi-tier PoC for LLM guardrails, then move it to AWS
evidence: Reported for a GovTech AI Engineer role (a search snippet, unverified): build a multi-tier proof-of-concept web app for LLM guardrails and describe its AWS architecture.
prompt: "Officers want to chat with an LLM, but we need guardrails on what goes in and what comes out. Sketch a multi-tier proof of concept, then tell me how you would run it on AWS for several agencies."

clarify.a: Personal data (NRIC numbers, phone numbers) reaching the model or the logs, prompt injection and jailbreaks, toxic output, and off-topic use.

clarify.q: Which model, and where does it run?
clarify.a: A hosted model through an API. We are not training or self-hosting one.
About 5,000 officers across a few agencies; maybe 50 chats at once at peak.
Yes, users expect tokens to stream.
Every blocked or flagged message, kept for a year, without storing raw personal data.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.ask: Separate what the PoC must show from what production needs.
steps.model:
• Functional: chat UI; input checks before the model sees a message; output checks before the user sees a reply; per-agency policies (which checks, thresholds, blocked topics); an audit log of guard decisions; an admin page to review flagged events.
  • Non-functional: input checks add under 300 ms at p95; streaming still works; fail closed on output personal-data checks; no raw personal data in logs; each agency's data isolated.
  • PoC scope: one agency, one model, deterministic checks plus one classifier, deployed with infrastructure as code so the move to production is a config change, not a rewrite.
  • Out of scope: fine-tuning, retrieval over agency documents (mention it as the next step).

steps.title: Estimates
steps.ask: Estimate traffic, tokens, guard latency budget and log volume.
steps.model:
• 5,000 officers × 20 messages a day = 100k messages/day, ~1.2/s average, ~12/s at a 10× peak.
  • ~1,500 tokens in and 500 out per message: ~200M tokens a day. Model cost, not compute, dominates the budget.
  • Guard latency per check type: regex and checksum ~1 ms; a small classifier on CPU ~20-50 ms; an LLM-as-judge call ~500 ms or more.
  • So the 300 ms budget fits deterministic checks plus 2-3 small classifiers, and LLM judging only for borderline cases.
  • Audit log: 100k × ~4 KB = ~400 MB/day, ~150 GB/year. Postgres for recent, S3 for the archive.

steps.title: API & data model
steps.ask: Define the API and the stored entities.
steps.model:
• POST /api/chat {conversationId, message} → server-sent events stream of tokens, ending with a guard summary.
  • GET /api/conversations/{id}.
  • GET/PUT /api/policies/{appId} (admin).
  • GET /api/guard-events?verdict=blocked&from= (admin).

Data (Postgres):

  • conversations, messages: store masked text only.
  • policies: JSON per app: enabled checks, thresholds, denied topics, fail mode.
  • guard_events: message_id, stage (input|output), check, score, verdict, latency_ms, policy_version, append-only.

Recording policy_version lets you explain later why a message was blocked. Streaming over server-sent events is simpler than WebSockets here: traffic is one-way after the request, it passes through load balancers as plain HTTP, and the browser reconnects on its own.

steps.title: High-level design
steps.ask: Draw the tiers and walk one message through them.
steps.model:
Three tiers: web (static React app), application (chat API + guardrail service), data (Postgres, Redis, object storage).

  1. Officer signs in through agency SSO (OIDC). The API checks the token and the agency's quota in Redis.
  2. The API sends the message to the guardrail service: mask personal data, run the injection classifier, run the topic filter.
  3. Blocked: return a refusal and write a guard event. Passed: send the masked prompt to the model.
  4. Tokens stream back through the guardrail service, which scans each sentence for personal data and toxicity before releasing it to the user.
  5. The API stores the masked conversation and guard events.

Keeping guards in their own service means any agency app can reuse them, and they can scale apart from the chat API.

steps.title: Deep dive
steps.ask: Go deep on the guard pipeline: ordering, streaming output, and how you know it works.
steps.model:
Tiered checks, cheapest first. Deterministic: NRIC/FIN pattern [STFGM]\d{7}[A-Z] plus its checksum, 8-digit phone numbers starting with 8 or 9, emails. Then small classifiers for injection and toxicity. Only scores in a grey band (say 0.4-0.7) go to an LLM judge. This keeps p95 low and cost bounded.

Reversible masking. Replace S1234567D with <NRIC_1>, keep the map in request memory only, and unmask in the reply only if policy allows.

Streaming output. Buffer about one sentence (~30-50 tokens), check it, then release. If a later sentence fails, stop the stream and replace it with a notice. Larger buffers are safer but feel slower.

Evaluation. Keep a red-team test set and track block rate and false-positive rate per check in CI.

steps.title: Bottlenecks & trade-offs
steps.ask: What would hurt in production on AWS, and what did you trade?
steps.model:
AWS layout: CloudFront + S3 for the web tier; ALB → ECS Fargate for the chat API and guardrail service in private subnets across 2 AZs; RDS Postgres Multi-AZ; ElastiCache Redis; secrets in Secrets Manager; model access through Bedrock over a VPC endpoint so prompts do not cross the public internet; CloudWatch alarms; Terraform or CDK for everything.

  • Model rate limits and latency: per-agency quotas, retries with backoff, a fallback model.
  • False positives annoy users: start new checks in shadow mode, log scores, tune thresholds per agency.
  • Fail closed vs open: closed for output personal data, open (with logging) for off-topic.
  • Cost: cache identical prompts; cap tokens per message.

rubric: Clarifies the concrete risks (personal data, injection, toxicity, off-topic) before designing.
Separates tiers clearly: web, application (with a distinct guardrail component), data.
Runs cheap deterministic checks before classifiers or LLM judges, with a latency budget.
Handles streamed output, not only the full reply.
Keeps raw personal data out of logs and storage (masking).
Records guard decisions with the policy version for audit.
Gives a concrete AWS layout: private subnets, managed database, secrets store, private model access.
Explains how guard quality is measured (test set, false-positive rate, shadow mode).

title: Backend for a government form submission system
evidence: Suggested by a prep guide (unverified) as a GovTech system design question; OGP runs FormSG, so interviewers may know the domain well.
prompt: "Design the backend for a government form submission system. Officers build forms; citizens fill them in, sometimes with attachments. Some forms get a huge spike when a scheme is announced on the news."

clarify.q: How many submissions, and how spiky?
clarify.a: About 1M a day normally. One announcement can bring 300k submissions in an hour.

clarify.q: Must the server be able to read the answers?
clarify.a: Not necessarily. Some agencies want answers emailed; others want them stored and are nervous about us reading them.
Up to 20 MB per submission. Mostly PDFs and photos.
Some need Singpass so we know who submitted.
Email, a dashboard for officers, or a webhook into the agency's own system.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.ask: Split the two workloads and list requirements for each.
steps.model:
• Form building (officers, low volume): create and edit a form schema, choose delivery (email or stored), set who can access it, publish.
  • Submission intake (citizens, bursty): load the form fast, validate answers, upload attachments, submit once even on double-click, get a reference number.
  • Delivery: email the response, or store it for a dashboard and CSV export, and optionally call an agency webhook.
  • Non-functional: survive 300k submissions in an hour; never lose an acknowledged submission; responses confidential, ideally unreadable by the platform; attachments virus-scanned; accessible on cheap phones.
  • Out of scope: payments, workflow approvals.

Say early: "Officers and citizens have very different traffic, so I'll scale them separately."

steps.title: Estimates
steps.ask: Size the spike, storage and webhook work.
steps.model:
• Normal: 1M/day ÷ 86,400 = ~12 submissions/s.
  • Spike: 300k in an hour = 83/s average, ~3× in the first minutes: ~250/s.
  • Form page loads: ~10 opens per submit → ~2.5k/s. Serve the form from a CDN.
  • Responses: 1M/day × 5 KB × 365 = ~1.8 TB/year.
  • Attachments: 10% × 1M × 2 MB = ~200 GB/day. Object storage, never the database.
  • Webhooks: 250/s × 0.2 s each = ~50 deliveries in flight.

Conclusion: 250 writes/s is easy for one database primary. The real risks are reads at the form page, large uploads through the API, and slow downstream systems.

steps.title: API & data model
steps.ask: Define the API and data model.
steps.model:
• POST /api/forms {title, fields[], mode, publicKey}: officer only. In storage mode only the public key is sent.
  • GET /api/forms/{id}: public schema, CDN-cached ~60 s.
  • POST /api/forms/{id}/attachments/presign {name, size, sha256} → a 5-minute upload URL.
  • POST /api/forms/{id}/submissions {submissionId, encryptedContent, attachmentKeys[]} → 201 {referenceId}; same submissionId again returns the same result.
  • GET /api/forms/{id}/submissions?after=: officer, pages of ciphertext.

Data: forms (document store; the schema is nested JSON that changes shape), submissions (form_id, submission_id unique, ciphertext, attachment keys, created_at), attachments in object storage, webhook_deliveries (status, attempts, next_try_at).

steps.title: High-level design
steps.ask: Draw the system and walk one submission.
steps.model:
1. Citizen opens the link: the form page and schema come from the CDN, not the API.
  2. If the form needs Singpass, the browser does the login redirect first.
  3. For each file, the browser asks for a presigned URL and uploads straight to object storage. A scanner picks up new objects and tags them clean or infected.
  4. In storage mode the browser encrypts the answers with the form's public key, then posts the ciphertext and file keys.
  5. A stateless, autoscaled API validates size and captcha, writes the submission in one insert, returns the reference number.
  6. It enqueues delivery jobs: email worker, webhook worker. Slow agencies never block the submit button.

Officers read submissions through the admin API and decrypt them in their own browser.

steps.title: Deep dive
steps.ask: Go deep on end-to-end encryption and reliable webhooks.
steps.model:
Encryption. When an officer creates a storage-mode form, the browser generates a key pair. The public key is stored with the form; the secret key is downloaded by the officer and never sent to the server. Citizens' browsers encrypt with the public key (FormSG uses tweetnacl for this). The platform stores only ciphertext, so a database leak exposes nothing readable. The cost: lose the key and the responses are gone, and the server cannot search or validate the content after encryption, so validate in the browser and again on structure only.

Webhooks. Sign each delivery (FormSG uses ed25519) over the body plus a timestamp; receivers reject anything older than ~5 minutes to stop replays. Deliver from a queue with exponential backoff for ~24 hours, then park in a dead-letter list the officer can see.

steps.title: Bottlenecks & trade-offs
steps.ask: What breaks first, and what did you trade?
steps.model:
• Announcement spike: CDN for page loads; autoscaling lags 1-3 minutes, so keep warm capacity before a known launch and add a waiting room for the worst cases.
  • Double submits: client-generated submissionId with a unique index.
  • Scan backlog: scanning after upload keeps submit fast but means an officer may briefly see "scan pending". Block download until clean.
  • Email limits: email providers throttle; queue and spread sends.
  • Email vs storage mode: email stores nothing (simplest, least liability) but responses are scattered in inboxes; storage mode gives a dashboard and webhooks but adds key management.
  • Document vs relational for forms: documents fit nested, changing schemas; submissions are append-only either way.

rubric: Separates form building (low volume) from submission intake (bursty) and scales them differently.
Serves the form page and schema from a CDN.
Uploads attachments directly to object storage with presigned URLs, and scans them.
Makes submit idempotent so a double-click does not create two submissions.
Explains client-side encryption and the lost-key trade-off.
Puts email and webhook delivery behind a queue with retries.
Signs webhooks and protects against replay.
Uses real numbers for the spike and storage.

title: Design a government link shortener
evidence: A common GovTech TAP / intern and OGP intern take-home (public GitHub repos); a GovTech GDS blog post (search snippet, undated) says it was tried as an interview exercise and later dropped, and OGP's go.gov.sg is a real government shortener.
prompt: "Design a link shortener for public officers, something like go.gov.sg. Officers create short links; the public clicks them in SMS messages and posters."

clarify.a: Only public officers. They log in with their government email and a one-time code.
Yes, officers usually want readable ones like go.gov.sg/vaccinate.
Use go.gov.sg's public figures: about 2.1M clicks a day and 8.7M links.

clarify.q: Can the destination change after printing?
clarify.a: Yes. The owner can edit or deactivate a link. Posters are already printed.
Click counts per day per link are enough.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.ask: List requirements. Call out what makes a government shortener different.
steps.model:
• Functional: officers log in by email OTP; create a link with a random or custom alias; edit the destination; deactivate; see daily clicks. The public visits /{alias} and is redirected.
  • Non-functional: redirects fast (~10 ms server time) and highly available, because links sit in national SMS blasts and printed posters; links never expire; aliases not guessable for random links.
  • Government twist: only officers create links, so citizens can trust the domain. Abuse means phishing targets, so destinations must be checkable and links quickly disabled.
  • Out of scope: QR generation (mention as a batch job), link-in-bio pages.

Reads dominate writes by thousands to one. Say so: it shapes the whole design.

steps.title: Estimates
steps.ask: Quick numbers: redirect rate, storage, key space.
steps.model:
• 2.1M clicks/day ÷ 86,400 = ~25 redirects/s average.
  • Peak ×20 when a link goes out in a national SMS: ~500/s.
  • 8.7M links × ~500 B = ~4.4 GB. Fits in one Postgres instance, and the hot set fits in Redis.
  • 7 base62 characters: 62^7 = 3.5 trillion keys. With 8.7M used, a random key collides about 1 time in 400,000, so retry-on-conflict is fine.

Conclusion: this is not a big-data problem. One primary database, a read replica and a cache handle it; spend the time on availability and abuse.

steps.title: API & data model
steps.ask: API and tables.
steps.model:
• POST /api/links {longUrl, alias?}: auth required, returns {shortUrl}, 409 if alias taken.
  • GET /{alias}: public, 302 to the destination, 404 if unknown or inactive.
  • PATCH /api/links/{alias} {longUrl?, active?}: owner only.
  • GET /api/links/{alias}/stats: daily counts.

Tables (Postgres):

  • links(short_id PK, long_url, owner_email, active, created_at, updated_at)
  • users(email PK, agency, created_at)
  • clicks_daily(short_id, day, count, PK(short_id, day))

The primary key on short_id is what guarantees two officers cannot claim the same alias. Keep clicks in their own daily table so the hot links rows are only read on redirect, never updated per click.

steps.title: High-level design
steps.ask: Draw the read path and the write path.
steps.model:
Write path: officer → load balancer → app → Postgres primary. The app generates a random 7-char key (or takes the custom alias) and inserts; on unique violation it retries with a new key or returns 409.

Read path: citizen → load balancer → app → Redis for alias → longUrl. On a miss, read the read replica (go.gov.sg's public README describes a replica serving redirects), fill Redis, return 302.

Clicks: increment a Redis counter per link per day on each redirect; a job flushes counters into clicks_daily every minute. No database write per click.

Use 302, not 301: browsers may cache a 301 indefinitely, so edits and deactivation would not take effect and clicks would go uncounted.

steps.title: Deep dive
steps.ask: Go deep: key generation and abuse.
steps.model:
Keys. Option 1: an auto-increment ID encoded in base62. Short and collision-free, but enumerable: anyone can walk every link, which may reveal unpublished announcements. Option 2: random 7 base62 characters with a unique constraint and retry. Not guessable; at 8.7M links collisions are rare. Pick option 2 for a government service.

Abuse. Only officers can create links, which already removes most spam. Still: check destinations against a malicious-URL list on create and periodically; let a security team deactivate any link instantly (delete the Redis key on update); show an interstitial for destinations outside approved domains; log who created and edited each link.

steps.title: Bottlenecks & trade-offs
steps.ask: What breaks, and what did you trade?
steps.model:
• Replica lag: an officer creates a link and tests it at once; the replica may not have it. On a replica miss, check the primary before returning 404.
  • Hot link in a national SMS: one Redis key takes all reads. Add a small in-process cache (a few seconds TTL) in each app instance.
  • Cache staleness after edits: delete the Redis key on every PATCH; keep TTLs short (~1 hour) as a backstop.
  • Redis down: fall back to the replica; 500/s is easy for Postgres.
  • Trade-off: 302 costs a server hit per click but keeps control and analytics.

rubric: Notes that reads dominate writes and designs a separate hot read path.
Estimates redirect QPS, storage and key space with real arithmetic.
Chooses 302 over 301 and explains why (editability, analytics).
Generates non-enumerable keys and handles collisions with a unique constraint.
Caches redirects and invalidates the cache on edit or deactivation.
Avoids a database write per click by batching counters.
Addresses phishing or abuse and who may create links.

title: Design a national vaccination booking system
evidence: OGP built Singapore's COVID-19 vaccination booking system and runs CalSG, whose public report notes a fix for overbooking when several people book one slot at once; a GovTech GDS blog snippet (undated) says a booking exercise was tried in interviews and dropped, so treat this as practice for contention and overload, not a current question.
prompt: "Design a national vaccination booking system. Residents are invited in waves by SMS and book two doses at a clinic they choose. Expect a rush the moment each wave opens."

clarify.q: How many people and how many slots?
clarify.a: About 5M people, two doses each. Around 40 centres.
A wave invites about 1M people. Many open the link in the first ten minutes.

clarify.q: Must the two doses be booked together?
clarify.a: Yes. Dose 2 must be 3 to 4 weeks after dose 1 at the same centre.
Only invited residents, once each. The invite link is personal.
Yes, and freed slots go back to the pool.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.ask: Requirements. Name the property that must never break.
steps.model:
• Functional: open a personal invite link; verify identity; browse centres and free slots; book dose 1 and dose 2 together; get an SMS confirmation; reschedule; cancel.
  • Non-functional: never overbook a slot and never give one person two bookings for the same dose, even under retries and bugs; stay up during the rush (degrade to a queue, not to errors); browsing may be a few seconds stale; booking must be exact.
  • Out of scope: clinic operations, vaccine stock, medical records.

Say: "Storage is tiny. The hard part is thousands of people fighting over the same few slots in the same minute."

steps.title: Estimates
steps.ask: Estimate the rush and what the backend must handle.
steps.model:
• Appointments: ~5M × 2 = ~10M.
  • Rush: 1M invited, 30% open in 10 minutes → 300k ÷ 600 s = ~500 arrivals/s, peaking near 2k/s.
  • A booking takes ~10 API calls. Size the API for ~3k req/s → admit ~300 people/s.
  • Everyone in the rush is through in 300k ÷ 300 = ~17 minutes. Acceptable with an honest queue screen.
  • Database: 300 bookings/s × 2 transactions = ~600 txn/s. One Postgres primary is enough.
  • Slots: dose 2 is 3-4 weeks out, so open ~6 weeks: 40 centres × 42 days × 24 half-hour windows = ~40k rows.
  • SMS: 1M invites ÷ 200 SMS/s = ~83 minutes on one sender. Pacing the send caps arrivals near the send rate; the rush above assumes a fast blast or news coverage.

steps.title: API & data model
steps.ask: API and data model. Show where correctness is enforced.
steps.model:
• GET /queue/status → position, or a signed pass valid 10 minutes.
  • GET /api/centres/{id}/availability?date=: cached, ~2 s stale.
  • POST /api/holds {slotIds[]} → 201 {holdId, expiresAt} or 409.
  • POST /api/bookings {holdId} + Idempotency-Key → 201, or 410 if the hold expired.
  • PATCH / DELETE /api/bookings/{id}.

Postgres:

  • slots(id, centre_id, starts_at, capacity, taken, CHECK (taken <= capacity))
  • holds(id, resident_id UNIQUE, slot_ids[], expires_at)
  • bookings(id, resident_id, dose_no, slot_id, status, idempotency_key UNIQUE) with a partial unique index on (resident_id, dose_no) where active.
  • invites(token_hash, resident_id, wave, used_at)

steps.title: High-level design
steps.ask: Draw the system and walk one booking.
steps.model:
1. Resident taps the SMS link. The CDN serves the static app; the app calls /queue/status.
  2. The waiting room (Redis: an arrival counter and an admitted-up-to pointer) returns a position until the pointer passes it, then a signed pass.
  3. With the pass, the app checks the invite and shows availability from a Redis view rebuilt every 2 s.
  4. The resident picks two slots. POST /holds runs one transaction: UPDATE slots SET taken = taken + 1 WHERE id = ANY($1) AND taken < capacity; if fewer than 2 rows changed, roll back and return 409.
  5. The resident confirms; the hold turns into two bookings in one transaction.
  6. A queue sends the SMS confirmation. A sweeper deletes expired holds and gives the seats back.

steps.title: Deep dive
steps.ask: Go deep on concurrency: why can this design never overbook?
steps.model:
Conditional UPDATE. taken < capacity is checked and changed in one statement. Postgres row locks serialise two transactions on the same slot; the second re-checks after the first commits, so it fails cleanly when the last seat is gone. No read-then-write race. Lock the two slots in id order (SELECT ... ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE) so two holds on the same pair cannot deadlock.

Belt and braces. The CHECK (taken <= capacity) constraint rejects overbooking even if someone writes buggy code later. The unique index on active (resident_id, dose_no) stops double bookings from two tabs.

Hold then confirm. Holding for 5 minutes stops people losing a slot while they read the screen. Expiry is a column, not a timer, so a crashed sweeper only delays release.

Why not lock in Redis? A second store means two sources of truth. At 600 txn/s, Postgres alone is simpler and exact.

steps.title: Bottlenecks & trade-offs
steps.ask: Bottlenecks and trade-offs.
steps.model:
• Hot slots: everyone wants Saturday morning at the nearest centre. Row locks queue up on a few rows; keep transactions tiny (no network calls inside) so each holds a lock for about a millisecond.
  • Waiting room vs autoscaling: autoscaling takes minutes and the database cannot scale out fast; a queue gives a fair, predictable wait.
  • Stale availability: browsing shows ~2 s old data, so a slot may vanish on confirm. Handle 409 with a friendly "just taken, here are the nearest free slots".
  • Retries: idempotency keys make a double-tap or a network retry return the same booking.
  • Fairness: first come first served rewards fast connections; staggered invite waves spread the load and the luck.

rubric: Identifies contention on a few slots, not data size, as the core problem.
Estimates the arrival rush and derives an admit rate from backend capacity.
Uses an atomic conditional update (or equivalent) so a slot is never overbooked.
Adds database constraints (CHECK, unique index) as a second line of defence.
Uses hold-then-confirm with expiry and explains how seats come back.
Uses a waiting room or queue to degrade gracefully instead of failing.
Makes booking idempotent across retries.
Handles stale availability honestly in the UX.

title: Design SMS OTP login at national scale
evidence: Scales up a reported GovTech/MOM pair-programming exercise (~2022, public GitHub repo) that asked for a small REST OTP server in one hour; no evidence this larger version is asked.
prompt: "You built a small OTP server earlier. Now design login with SMS one-time codes for a national identity service that dozens of agency apps rely on."

clarify.a: About 4.5M accounts, ~3M logins a day, with spikes when a payout or deadline opens.

clarify.q: Do agency apps see the code?
clarify.a: No. They should get a verified identity without handling secrets.

clarify.q: How long is a code valid, and how many tries?
clarify.a: Your call, but justify it.

clarify.q: What about phone numbers that are not registered?
clarify.a: Don't let attackers find out which numbers are registered.
We have one today; a second is possible.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.ask: Requirements, including security ones.
steps.model:
• Functional: request a 6-digit code by phone; verify it; resend with a cooldown; create a session; let agency apps sign users in by redirect and receive a signed identity token.
  • Security: codes are random, single-use, expire in 5 minutes; at most 5 wrong attempts per code; no way to tell registered from unregistered numbers; codes never stored in plain text or logged; rate limits per phone, per IP and globally to stop SMS cost attacks.
  • Non-functional: survive ~700 logins/s at peak; SMS delivered within ~10 s; the identity service is critical, so multi-AZ and no single provider dependency.
  • Out of scope: account registration, biometric app login (mention as safer).

steps.title: Estimates
steps.ask: Estimate load, SMS volume, guess odds and memory.
steps.model:
• 4.5M accounts × ~0.7 logins/day = ~3M logins/day, ~35/s average.
  • ×20 at a payout opening: ~700/s.
  • Half use SMS, 10% resend: 3M × 0.5 × 1.1 = ~1.65M SMS/day. SMS cost is a real budget line, which is why abuse limits matter.
  • Guessing: 5 attempts against 10^6 codes = 1 in 200,000 per code. Per-phone request limits bound total tries.
  • Live codes in Redis: 700/s × 300 s × ~300 B = ~63 MB.

Conclusion: compute is easy. The design is about security limits, SMS reliability and the identity protocol.

steps.title: API & data model
steps.ask: API and data model.
steps.model:
• POST /otp {phone} → always 202 {txnId} with the same message, registered or not; 429 when limited.
  • POST /otp/verify {txnId, code} → 200 + HttpOnly session cookie; 401 wrong; 410 expired; 423 too many attempts.
  • GET /authorize?client_id&redirect_uri&state&nonce&code_challenge (OIDC).
  • POST /token {code, code_verifier, client_assertion} → signed ID token.
  • GET /.well-known/jwks.json.

Data: Redis otp:{txnId} → {phone, hmac(code), attempts} TTL 300 s; Redis rate counters per phone and IP; Postgres users, clients (agency apps, redirect URIs, public keys), login_audit; sessions in Redis with a 30-minute idle TTL.

steps.title: High-level design
steps.ask: Draw it and walk one agency login.
steps.model:
1. User clicks "Log in" in an agency app. The app redirects to /authorize with a PKCE challenge.
  2. The identity service shows the login page. User enters a phone; POST /otp checks rate limits, creates the code, stores its HMAC in Redis and puts an SMS job on a queue.
  3. An SMS worker sends through the provider and records the delivery receipt.
  4. User enters the code; /otp/verify compares HMACs in constant time, deletes the code, creates a session.
  5. The service redirects back to the agency app with a one-time code.
  6. The agency backend calls /token with the PKCE verifier and its signed client assertion, gets an ID token, verifies it with the JWKS keys.

Agency apps never see the OTP or the user's password-equivalent.

steps.title: Deep dive
steps.ask: Go deep on OTP safety.
steps.model:
• Generation: 6 digits from a cryptographically secure random generator, never random.random().
  • Storage: store HMAC(server_key, txnId + code), not the code. A Redis dump is useless without the key, and a plain hash of 6 digits is brute-forced in milliseconds.
  • Single use: delete on success with an atomic script so two parallel verifies cannot both win.
  • Attempts: increment before comparing; at 5, kill the code (not the account), so an attacker cannot lock real users out.
  • Requests: one resend per 30 s, 5 per phone per hour, per-IP and per-country limits; a global SMS budget alarm catches SMS pumping fraud.
  • Enumeration: identical response and timing for unknown numbers.
  • Compare in constant time.

steps.title: Bottlenecks & trade-offs
steps.ask: Bottlenecks, risks and trade-offs.
steps.model:
• SMS provider outage: the biggest single point of failure. Use two providers, fail over on error rate or delivery-receipt lag, and offer app-based login as an alternative.
  • SIM swap and phishing: SMS OTP can be phished in real time by a fake site. Push approval in an app bound to the device is stronger; keep SMS as a fallback.
  • Lockout vs brute force: locking accounts lets attackers lock out victims; limit per code and per source instead.
  • Sessions: server-side session IDs can be revoked instantly; stateless JWTs scale without lookups but cannot be revoked before expiry. For a national identity service, prefer revocable sessions.
  • Redis: replicate across AZs; losing it only forces users to request a new code.

rubric: Stores only a keyed hash (HMAC) of the code, with a short TTL.
Makes codes single-use and limits verify attempts per code.
Rate-limits code requests per phone and per IP, and mentions SMS cost abuse.
Prevents phone-number enumeration with identical responses.
Uses a standard federation protocol (OIDC authorization code with PKCE) for agency apps.
Sends SMS through a queue and plans for provider failure.
Discusses SMS weaknesses (SIM swap, real-time phishing) and a stronger alternative.
Chooses lockout behaviour that does not let attackers lock out real users.

title: Design a bulk messaging service for agencies
evidence: OGP runs Postman.gov.sg for agency mass messaging and publishes how its sender works; there is no evidence GovTech asks this as an interview question.
prompt: "Agencies upload a CSV of recipients and a message template, then send a campaign by SMS or email. One campaign can have a million recipients. Design it."

clarify.a: Yes. The template has fields like {{name}} filled from CSV columns.

clarify.q: Is a duplicate worse than a missed message?
clarify.a: Yes. Sending a million citizens the same SMS twice is worse than missing a handful.
Assume one sender can push about 200 messages a second to a provider.
Yes: sent, delivered, failed, per recipient, and campaign totals.

clarify.q: Can a campaign be stopped midway?
clarify.a: Yes, quickly, if the message has a mistake.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.ask: Requirements. State the delivery guarantee you will aim for.
steps.model:
• Functional: create a campaign (channel, template, sender credentials); upload a CSV; validate it and preview a rendered message; send now or later; stop; see per-recipient status and totals; export failures.
  • Delivery guarantee: at most once per recipient as the default. Under-sending is preferred to over-sending; failures are reported, not blindly retried.
  • Non-functional: 1M messages in under ~30 minutes when providers allow; one agency's campaign must not starve another's; credentials encrypted; recipient data deleted after a retention period.
  • Out of scope: two-way replies, marketing analytics.

steps.title: Estimates
steps.ask: Estimate send time, worker count, storage and callbacks.
steps.model:
• One worker at ~200 msg/s: 1M ÷ 200 = 5,000 s ≈ 83 minutes. Too slow for urgent alerts.
  • 5 workers sharing a campaign: ~17 minutes, if the provider account allows 1,000/s. Postman reported sending 1M WhatsApp messages in 22 minutes during COVID, about 760/s.
  • CSV: 1M rows × ~100 B = ~100 MB. Upload to object storage, not through the API.
  • Message rows: 1M × ~500 B = ~500 MB per campaign. Partition or archive by campaign.
  • Delivery callbacks arrive at about the send rate: ~1k/s bursts. Handle them with serverless functions behind a queue.

steps.title: API & data model
steps.ask: API and data model, including job states.
steps.model:
• POST /campaigns {channel, template}
  • POST /campaigns/{id}/upload-url → presigned URL; POST /campaigns/{id}/process validates the CSV.
  • POST /campaigns/{id}/send, POST /campaigns/{id}/stop
  • GET /campaigns/{id}/stats
  • POST /callbacks/{provider}: signed provider callbacks.

Postgres:

  • campaigns(id, agency, channel, template, status, credential_ref)
  • messages(campaign_id, recipient, params, message_id, dequeued_at, sent_at, delivered_at, error)
  • job_queue(id, campaign_id, worker_id, status, send_rate) with states READY → ENQUEUED → SENDING → SENT or STOPPED → LOGGED (the states Postman documents).

Keeping one row per recipient is what makes status, stop and safe retries possible: every message has its own record of whether it left, when, and the provider's ID. Credentials live in a secrets store; the campaign holds only a reference.

steps.title: High-level design
steps.ask: Draw the system and walk one campaign.
steps.model:
1. The agency uploads the CSV straight to object storage. A parser worker validates rows, renders a preview and bulk-inserts messages.
  2. Pressing send inserts a job_queue row in READY.
  3. Sender workers poll the table. A worker claims a job inside a transaction (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED), so only one worker takes it.
  4. The worker takes batches of ~1,000 messages, marks dequeued_at, sends each through the provider at its rate, and saves the provider's message_id.
  5. Providers post delivery results to callback functions, which update delivered_at or error.
  6. When nothing is left, the job moves to SENT; a logger worker computes totals and moves it to LOGGED.

steps.title: Deep dive
steps.ask: Go deep on not sending duplicates when workers crash.
steps.model:
Exactly-once is impossible over a provider API: a worker can crash after the provider accepted a message but before saving the message_id. So choose which way to fail.

  • Before sending, mark the message dequeued_at = now() in the same batch claim, so no other worker picks it.
  • After the provider accepts, save message_id.
  • After a crash, do not resend dequeued messages automatically: the worker may already have sent them. They stay unsent, which under-sends.
  • When the agency retries, clear dequeued_at only for messages with no message_id, the rule Postman documents. Anything the provider confirmed is never resent.
  • The remaining risk is the tiny window between acceptance and saving the id: a retry can resend those few. Save each id right after its send to keep the window small.

Stop: workers re-read the job status between batches, so a stop takes effect within one batch (~5 s at 200/s).

steps.title: Bottlenecks & trade-offs
steps.ask: Bottlenecks and trade-offs.
steps.model:
• Provider rate limits: a token bucket per provider credential, shared by all workers on that campaign. Exceeding it gets you throttled or blocked.
  • Database as queue: simple, transactional and visible to ops; fine at a few thousand updates a second if you update in batches. Past that, move dispatch to a real queue (SQS, Kafka) and keep Postgres for state.
  • Fairness: cap workers per agency so one million-recipient campaign does not block a small urgent one.
  • Callback storms: serverless handlers absorb bursts; batch the database updates.
  • Bad CSVs: reject on validation with row numbers, before anything is sent.
  • At-most-once vs at-least-once: right for broadcast messages; wrong for, say, payment reminders where a miss is costly.

rubric: States a delivery guarantee (at most once, under-send preferred) and justifies it.
Computes send time from a per-worker rate and scales workers to meet a target.
Uploads the CSV to object storage and validates before sending.
Claims jobs atomically so two workers never send the same batch.
Explains crash recovery: resend only messages without a provider message ID.
Supports a fast stop that workers check between batches.
Rate-limits per provider credential and keeps agencies from starving each other.
Handles delivery callbacks asynchronously.

title: Design a ride-hailing service like Uber
evidence: A widely used industry system design question; no source ties it to GovTech or OGP, so practise it for the patterns it teaches (geospatial search, matching, live location).
prompt: "Design a ride-hailing app like Uber or Grab. A rider requests a ride, nearby drivers get an offer, and both see each other's live location until the trip ends."

clarify.a: About 1M drivers online at peak worldwide and 10M rides a day.

clarify.q: How often do drivers send location?
clarify.a: Every 4 seconds while online.
Mention surge pricing briefly. Payments are out of scope.

clarify.q: Offer one driver at a time or many?
clarify.a: Your call. Explain the trade-off.
Yes. A ride never crosses cities.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.ask: Requirements for rider, driver and the system.
steps.model:
• Rider: see nearby cars and an ETA; request a ride from pickup to drop-off; get matched; watch the driver approach; trip history.
  • Driver: go online; stream location; receive an offer and accept or decline within ~15 s; navigate; complete the trip.
  • Non-functional: match within ~10 s; a driver is never assigned two rides at once; location shown within a few seconds; the location firehose must not overload durable storage; partition by city so one city's outage stays local.
  • Out of scope: payments, ratings, driver onboarding.

Two very different data types: ephemeral, high-rate locations and durable, low-rate trips. Say you will store them differently.

steps.title: Estimates
steps.ask: Estimate location writes, ride rate, connections and storage.
steps.model:
• Location: 1M drivers ÷ 4 s = 250k updates/s. At ~100 B each, ~25 MB/s.
  • Rides: 10M/day ÷ 86,400 = ~115/s, ~350/s at a 3× peak.
  • Open connections: 1M drivers + ~2M riders in-app ≈ 3M WebSockets; at ~50k per server, ~60 gateway servers.
  • Trips: 10M × 2 KB = ~20 GB/day.
  • Full GPS trails if kept: 250k/s × 100 B × 86,400 = ~2 TB/day. Keep only trip-time points, sampled.

Conclusion: locations must live in memory, not a database row per ping. Ride writes are modest and can use a relational store sharded by city.

steps.title: API & data model
steps.ask: API and data model.
steps.model:
• Driver WebSocket: location {lat, lng, heading, ts} every 4 s; server pushes offer {rideId, pickup, expiresIn}.
  • POST /rides {pickup, dropoff, product} → {rideId, status: MATCHING}.
  • POST /rides/{id}/accept, /arrived, /start, /complete.
  • Rider WebSocket: ride status and driver location.

Data:

  • Geo index (in memory, per city): cell → set of available driver IDs; driver → last location and cell.
  • Rides (Postgres or MySQL, sharded by city): id, rider_id, driver_id, status, pickup, dropoff, fare, timestamps.
  • Location stream (Kafka) for ETA, surge and trip trails.

steps.title: High-level design
steps.ask: Draw the system and walk a ride request.
steps.model:
1. Drivers' apps hold a WebSocket to a gateway. Each location goes to the location service, which updates the in-memory geo index for that city and publishes to Kafka.
  2. Rider posts a ride. The ride service writes it as MATCHING and calls dispatch.
  3. Dispatch asks the geo index for available drivers within ~2 km, then asks the maps/ETA service for road ETAs and ranks them.
  4. It locks the best driver and sends an offer through the gateway. Accept: ride becomes ACCEPTED. Decline or 15 s timeout: unlock, try the next.
  5. During the trip, driver locations are forwarded to the rider's connection.
  6. Consumers of the Kafka stream compute surge per area and store trip trails.

steps.title: Deep dive
steps.ask: Go deep on finding nearby drivers fast.
steps.model:
Geohash. Encode lat/lng as a string where a shared prefix means nearby. Pick a precision whose cell is at least the search radius: precision 5 cells are about 4.9 km × 4.9 km, precision 6 about 1.2 km × 0.6 km. For 2 km use precision 5 and look up the rider's cell and its 8 neighbours, because a driver 50 m away can sit across a cell border. Filter by exact distance, then rank by road ETA, not straight-line distance.

Updates. Each ping, if the driver's cell changed, remove them from the old cell set and add to the new one. That is two O(1) set operations, so 250k/s is fine spread over a few dozen in-memory shards keyed by city and cell.

Alternatives. H3 hexagons (all neighbours equidistant) or S2 cells; a quadtree adapts cell size to density.

No double dispatch. Lock the driver with an atomic set-if-absent and a 15 s TTL before sending an offer.

steps.title: Bottlenecks & trade-offs
steps.ask: Bottlenecks and trade-offs.
steps.model:
• Location firehose: never write each ping to a database. Memory for current state, Kafka for history, sampling for storage.
  • Hot cells: airports and stadiums pack thousands of drivers in one cell. Use finer cells there or adaptive structures.
  • One offer at a time vs broadcast: sequential offers are fair and avoid races but add up to 15 s per decline; broadcasting to 3 drivers matches faster but wastes drivers' attention. Many systems batch-match requests every few seconds for a better global result.
  • Geo index node dies: state rebuilds within 4 s from the next pings; no durable copy needed.
  • Consistency: ride state needs strong consistency (one driver per ride); locations can be eventually consistent.

rubric: Separates ephemeral high-rate location data from durable trip data.
Estimates location update rate and concludes it must stay in memory.
Uses a geospatial index (geohash, quadtree, H3 or S2) and searches neighbouring cells.
Ranks candidates by road ETA, not straight-line distance.
Prevents a driver from being offered two rides at once (lock with TTL).
Uses persistent connections (WebSocket) for driver offers and live tracking.
Partitions by city or region.
Discusses a matching trade-off (sequential offers vs broadcast or batch matching).

title: Design a video streaming service like Netflix
evidence: A widely used industry system design question; no source ties it to GovTech or OGP, so practise it for the patterns it teaches (CDNs, transcoding pipelines, adaptive bitrate).
prompt: "Design a video streaming service like Netflix. Studios deliver films; members browse, press play, and watch on phones, laptops and TVs."

clarify.a: About 200M members; peak evening concurrency around 30M streams.
No. A curated catalogue delivered by studios.
Out of scope. On demand only.
Playback start time and no rebuffering. Recommendations briefly.
Yes, studios require it.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.ask: Requirements. Separate the content pipeline from playback.
steps.model:
• Content pipeline: ingest a studio master file, transcode it into many resolutions and codecs, package for streaming, encrypt, and distribute before release day.
  • Member side: browse personalised rows; search; press play and start in under ~2 s; adapt quality to bandwidth; resume where you left off on any device; DRM.
  • Non-functional: rebuffering rare; video traffic is the giant, so egress cost dominates; control-plane APIs highly available (degrade to a generic home page rather than fail).
  • Out of scope: live events, user uploads, billing.

Point out early: the control plane (browse, play API) is ordinary microservices; the data plane (video bytes) is a CDN problem.

steps.title: Estimates
steps.ask: Estimate bandwidth, storage and control-plane load.
steps.model:
• Peak 30M streams × ~5 Mbps = ~150 Tbps. No single data centre can serve that; it must come from edge caches near viewers.
  • Catalogue: assume 20k titles × ~1.5 hours. A full ladder (around 10 bitrates × 2-3 codecs) is roughly 30 GB per hour of content: 20k × 1.5 × 30 GB = ~900 TB. Small enough to copy the popular part to every edge site.
  • Playback API: 30M streams start over ~3 evening hours: ~3k plays/s average, ~10k/s at peaks.
  • Heartbeats every 30 s for resume: 30M ÷ 30 = ~1M writes/s. Needs a write-optimised store.

steps.title: API & data model
steps.ask: API and data model.
steps.model:
• GET /home?profile= → personalised rows of title IDs.
  • GET /titles/{id} → metadata, artwork.
  • POST /play {titleId, device, capabilities} → manifest URL on the best edge, DRM licence URL, resume position.
  • POST /license → decryption key for this device.
  • POST /events/progress {titleId, positionSec} every 30 s.

Data:

  • Catalogue (relational, cached heavily): titles, episodes, rights per country.
  • Viewing history (Cassandra, partitioned by profile, newest first): fits ~1M writes/s.
  • Video assets in object storage: segments of ~4 s per bitrate, plus manifests; copies on edge caches.
  • Recommendations: precomputed rows per profile, refreshed offline.

steps.title: High-level design
steps.ask: Draw both paths: ingest and playback.
steps.model:
Ingest: studio master → object storage → split into chunks → hundreds of parallel transcode workers → package into DASH/HLS segments → encrypt → store → push to edge caches overnight, ahead of demand.

Playback:

  1. The app calls the API gateway for the home page; services return cached rows.
  2. Member presses play. The playback service checks entitlement and country rights, picks the healthiest nearby edge for this client, and returns a manifest and licence URL.
  3. The player gets a DRM licence, then fetches segments directly from the edge, never from the origin.
  4. The player measures throughput and buffer and switches bitrate segment by segment.
  5. Progress events flow to the history store for resume and recommendations.

steps.title: Deep dive
steps.ask: Go deep on getting bytes to viewers without rebuffering.
steps.model:
Edge placement. Put cache servers inside ISPs and at internet exchanges (Netflix's version is called Open Connect). Video then crosses one short hop, which cuts cost and latency.

Pre-positioning. Popularity is predictable: tomorrow's hits are known tonight. Fill edges during off-peak hours, so peak evening traffic is almost all cache hits. The long tail is fetched from regional caches on a miss.

Adaptive bitrate. Each title is cut into ~4 s segments at many bitrates. The player starts at a low bitrate for a fast start, then picks the highest bitrate its buffer and measured throughput can sustain. If the buffer drains, it steps down instead of stalling.

Per-title encoding. A cartoon needs far fewer bits than an action film at the same quality, so tune the ladder per title and save bandwidth.

steps.title: Bottlenecks & trade-offs
steps.ask: Bottlenecks and trade-offs.
steps.model:
• Egress cost: solved by ISP-embedded caches, pre-positioning and efficient codecs (newer codecs need fewer bits but more encode time and device support).
  • New release spike: pre-warm every edge before launch.
  • Transcode cost: chunk-parallel encoding finishes a film in minutes; it is a one-off per title, so spend compute here to save bandwidth forever.
  • Control-plane failure: if recommendations fail, serve a cached or generic home page; if history fails, play from the start. Fallbacks beat errors.
  • Heartbeat writes: ~1M/s suits Cassandra's write path; strong consistency is not needed for resume points.
  • Segment length: shorter segments adapt faster but mean more requests and less efficient compression.

rubric: Separates the control plane (APIs) from the data plane (video bytes on a CDN).
Estimates peak bandwidth and concludes it must be served from the edge.
Describes an ingest pipeline: chunked parallel transcoding, packaging, encryption.
Explains adaptive bitrate with segments at multiple bitrates.
Pre-positions popular content on edges before demand.
Stores viewing progress in a write-optimised store.
Plans graceful fallbacks for failing services.
Mentions DRM and licence issuance.

title: Design a social news feed
evidence: A widely used industry system design question; no source ties it to GovTech or OGP, so practise it for the patterns it teaches (fan-out on write versus read, caching, ranking).
prompt: "Design the home feed for a social network like Twitter or Facebook. Users follow others and see recent posts from them, newest or best first."

clarify.a: 300M daily active users, each opening the feed about 10 times a day.
Average 200. Some accounts have 50M followers.
Start chronological, then tell me how ranking fits.
Posts can have images; assume they live in object storage and a CDN.
A new post should appear in followers' feeds within a few seconds.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.ask: Requirements.
steps.model:
• Functional: create a post; follow and unfollow; load the home feed with pagination; feed contains posts from followed accounts.
  • Non-functional: feed loads in ~200 ms at p99; posts appear within ~5 s; reads vastly outnumber writes; feed can be eventually consistent (a missing post for a few seconds is fine); celebrity posts must not melt the system.
  • Out of scope: comments, likes counting, notifications, search, ads.

The core question is when to build each user's feed: when a post is written (fan-out on write) or when a feed is read (fan-out on read). Say you will compare them with numbers.

steps.title: Estimates
steps.ask: Estimate reads, writes, fan-out and cache size.
steps.model:
• Feed reads: 300M × 10 = 3B/day ≈ 35k/s, ~100k/s at peak.
  • Posts: 300M × 0.5 = 150M/day ≈ 1.7k/s.
  • Fan-out on write: 1.7k posts/s × 200 followers = ~350k feed inserts/s. High but spreadable across a cache cluster.
  • A celebrity post: 50M inserts for one post. At 350k/s that alone takes ~2.5 minutes. This breaks pure push.
  • Feed cache: 300M users × 500 post IDs × 8 B = ~1.2 TB raw, more with Redis overhead, sharded across ~20-40 nodes.

Conclusion: push for normal accounts, pull for celebrities.

steps.title: API & data model
steps.ask: API and data model.
steps.model:
• POST /posts {text, mediaIds[]} → {postId}
  • GET /feed?cursor=&limit=20 → posts plus nextCursor
  • POST /follow/{userId}, DELETE /follow/{userId}

Data:

  • posts: sharded by post_id; ID is time-sortable (Snowflake-style: timestamp + machine + sequence) so ordering needs no extra column.
  • follows: two tables, followers(user_id → follower_id) and following(user_id → followee_id), each sharded by its first column.
  • feed cache: Redis list per user of the latest ~500 post IDs.
  • post cache: post ID → post object, so a feed page is one list read plus a multi-get.

Use a cursor (last post ID seen), not an offset, so new posts do not shift pages.

steps.title: High-level design
steps.ask: Draw the write path and the read path.
steps.model:
Write:

  1. Post service stores the post and returns at once.
  2. It publishes a "new post" event to a queue.
  3. Fan-out workers look up the author's followers in pages and push the post ID onto each follower's Redis feed list, trimming to 500.
  4. Authors with more than ~10k followers are flagged as celebrities and skipped.

Read:

  1. Feed service reads the user's precomputed list from Redis.
  2. It fetches recent posts from the celebrities that user follows (usually a handful) and merges by ID.
  3. It hydrates post objects from the post cache, filters deleted or blocked content, and returns 20 with a cursor.

Inactive users (not seen in 30 days) are skipped in fan-out; their feed is built on demand when they return.

steps.title: Deep dive
steps.ask: Go deep on the hybrid fan-out and on ranking.
steps.model:
Why hybrid. Pure push makes reads one cache lookup but a celebrity post costs 50M writes and minutes of lag. Pure pull makes writes free but every read must query 200 followees and merge, about 200 lookups at 100k reads/s. Hybrid pays push cost only for the ~99% of accounts with modest audiences and pull cost only for the few celebrities a user follows.

Threshold. Pick it from numbers, e.g. 10k followers, and tune by measuring fan-out lag and read latency.

Ranking. Stage 1, candidates: the ~500 IDs from the hybrid feed. Stage 2, score each with a light model (author affinity, recency, engagement so far, media type). Stage 3, re-rank for diversity (not five posts from one author in a row). Cache the ranked page briefly so scrolling is stable.

steps.title: Bottlenecks & trade-offs
steps.ask: Bottlenecks and trade-offs.
steps.model:
• Fan-out lag during spikes: the queue absorbs it; feeds become a few seconds stale, which is acceptable.
  • Hot celebrity post read by millions: post-object cache with replicas, plus a short in-process cache.
  • Cache loss: a lost Redis shard means rebuilding feeds by pull on next read; slower, not broken.
  • Unfollow and deletes: filter at read time rather than rewriting millions of lists.
  • Memory: keep only IDs in feed lists and cap at 500; older pages fall back to pull.
  • Consistency: eventual consistency for feeds; strong only for the post itself and follow edges.

rubric: Compares fan-out on write and fan-out on read with numbers.
Identifies the celebrity problem and proposes a hybrid.
Stores post IDs (not full posts) in per-user feed lists, capped in length.
Uses cursor-based pagination with time-sortable IDs.
Does fan-out asynchronously through a queue.
Skips or defers fan-out for inactive users.
Explains where ranking fits (candidates, scoring, re-ranking).
States which parts can be eventually consistent.

title: Design a chat app like WhatsApp
evidence: A widely used industry system design question; no source ties it to GovTech or OGP, so practise it for the patterns it teaches (persistent connections, ordering, delivery guarantees).
prompt: "Design a messaging app like WhatsApp or Telegram: one-to-one and group chats, delivered instantly when online and later when offline."

clarify.a: 500M daily users, about 40 messages each per day.
Up to 256 members.
Yes: sent, delivered, read, and online or last seen.
Keep it until every device has it; assume history sync for new devices is out of scope.
Yes, but don't design the cryptography. Tell me how it affects the server.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.ask: Requirements.
steps.model:
• Functional: send text (media via upload link) to a person or group; deliver in real time if the recipient is online, otherwise on reconnect plus a push notification; receipts (sent, delivered, read); presence; message order preserved within a chat.
  • Non-functional: delivery in ~200 ms when both are online; no message lost once the server acknowledged it; no duplicates shown; works on flaky mobile networks; end-to-end encrypted, so the server routes ciphertext it cannot read.
  • Out of scope: calls, stories, full history sync, search.

Two hard parts to call out: keeping millions of connections open, and delivering exactly once from the user's point of view over an unreliable network.

steps.title: Estimates
steps.ask: Estimate message rate, connections and storage.
steps.model:
• 500M × 40 = 20B messages/day ≈ 230k/s average, ~700k/s at peak.
  • Concurrent connections: assume 40% online at peak = 200M. At ~100k per tuned gateway server, ~2,000 servers.
  • Storage: 20B × ~100 B = ~2 TB/day before replication. Delete after delivery to all devices, or keep ~30 days as a buffer.
  • Group fan-out: if 20% of messages go to groups of ~20, deliveries ≈ 20B × (0.8 + 0.2 × 20) = ~96B deliveries/day.
  • Presence: each heartbeat every 30 s = 200M ÷ 30 ≈ ~7M/s if done naively. That is why presence needs care.

steps.title: API & data model
steps.ask: Protocol and data model.
steps.model:
• WebSocket (or MQTT) per device. Client → server: send {clientMsgId, chatId, ciphertext}; server → client: ack {clientMsgId, seq}; server → recipient: msg {chatId, seq, sender, ciphertext}; recipient → server: delivered {chatId, upToSeq}, read {chatId, upToSeq}.
  • GET /chats/{id}/messages?afterSeq= for catch-up on reconnect.

Data:

  • messages (Cassandra): partition key chat_id, clustering key seq. One chat's messages live together, already ordered.
  • chat members: chat → member list.
  • delivery cursors: (user, chat) → last delivered and read seq.
  • session registry (Redis): user/device → gateway server, with a TTL.
  • presence (Redis): user → last seen, TTL.

steps.title: High-level design
steps.ask: Draw it and walk a message from Alice to Bob.
steps.model:
1. Alice's phone holds a WebSocket to gateway G1. It sends the encrypted message with a random clientMsgId.
  2. G1 forwards to the chat service, which assigns the next seq for the chat, writes it to the message store, and acks Alice: one tick.
  3. The chat service looks up Bob in the session registry: he is on gateway G7. It sends the message to G7, which pushes it to Bob's phone.
  4. Bob's phone acks delivered upToSeq; the receipt flows back to Alice: two ticks.
  5. If Bob is offline, the message stays stored and a push notification goes through APNs/FCM. On reconnect, Bob's app asks for everything after its last seq.

For groups, the chat service writes once and fans out delivery to each member's gateway through a queue.

steps.title: Deep dive
steps.ask: Go deep on ordering and exactly-once delivery from the user's view.
steps.model:
Ordering. Wall clocks on phones disagree, so do not sort by timestamps. Give each chat a monotonic sequence number assigned by one owner: route all writes for a chat to the same chat-service shard (hash of chat ID), which increments a counter. Clients display by seq.

No loss. The server acks only after the message is durably written. If Alice gets no ack, she resends.

No duplicates. A resend carries the same clientMsgId; the server keeps recent IDs per chat and returns the original seq instead of writing again. Delivery to Bob is at least once (pushed, then fetched on reconnect); Bob's app drops any seq it already has. At-least-once transport plus idempotent receivers gives exactly-once display.

Encryption. With end-to-end encryption, groups use sender keys so a message is encrypted once, not 256 times.

steps.title: Bottlenecks & trade-offs
steps.ask: Bottlenecks and trade-offs.
steps.model:
• Reconnect storms: deploying a gateway drops 100k connections at once. Drain slowly and have clients reconnect with random jitter.
  • Presence chatter: do not broadcast every status change to every contact. Fetch presence when a chat is opened and subscribe only while it is visible.
  • Large groups: fan-out cost grows with members; cap groups or switch very large ones to pull on open.
  • Hot chat partition: a very busy group lands on one partition; acceptable at 256 members, a problem for broadcast channels.
  • WebSocket vs polling: long-lived connections cost memory per user but give instant delivery and save battery compared with frequent polling.
  • Storage: deleting after delivery saves cost and limits exposure, at the price of no server-side history.

rubric: Uses persistent connections and a session registry to find the recipient's gateway.
Sizes connections and gateway servers with numbers.
Orders messages with a per-chat sequence number, not device clocks.
Acks only after a durable write; deduplicates retries with a client message ID.
Handles offline users with stored messages, catch-up by sequence, and push notifications.
Partitions message storage by chat ID.
Addresses group fan-out cost.
Mentions reconnect storms or presence traffic as a scaling problem.

title: Design a distributed key-value store
evidence: A widely used industry system design question; no source ties it to GovTech or OGP, so practise it for the patterns it teaches (partitioning, replication, quorums, conflict handling).
prompt: "Design a distributed key-value store like Amazon's Dynamo or Cassandra. put(key, value) and get(key), across many machines, and it must keep working when machines fail."

clarify.a: About 10 TB of data, values around 1 KB, up to 1 MB.
100k writes and 300k reads a second.

clarify.q: Consistency or availability during a network split?
clarify.a: Writes should keep working; tunable consistency is a plus.
No. Point lookups only.
Yes, three availability zones.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.ask: Requirements, including the CAP position.
steps.model:
• Functional: put, get, delete by key; per-request consistency level; add and remove nodes without downtime.
  • Non-functional: p99 under ~10 ms; survives a node or an availability zone failure; data replicated 3 times; scales linearly by adding nodes; available under partition (AP), with tunable consistency through quorums.
  • Out of scope: transactions across keys, secondary indexes, range scans.

Say the choice explicitly: "Writes must keep working during a split, so I'll pick availability and handle conflicts, with quorum settings to get stronger reads when callers need them."

steps.title: Estimates
steps.ask: Size the cluster.
steps.model:
• 10 TB × 3 replicas = 30 TB stored.
  • At ~2 TB usable per node (leave half the disk for compaction and growth): 15 nodes; run ~20 for headroom.
  • Traffic: 100k writes/s × 3 replicas = 300k replica writes/s; reads at quorum 2 = 600k replica reads/s. Over 20 nodes: ~15k writes and ~30k reads per node per second. An LSM-tree node on SSD handles that.
  • Network: 100k × 1 KB × 3 = ~300 MB/s cluster-wide replication traffic.
  • Adding one node moves about 1/20 of the data, ~1.5 TB, at a throttled ~100 MB/s: ~4 hours.

steps.title: API & data model
steps.ask: API and on-node data layout.
steps.model:
• PUT /kv/{key} body = value, header context (version from a previous get); query w=2.
  • GET /kv/{key}?r=2 → value(s) + context. If replicas disagree, may return siblings.
  • DELETE /kv/{key} writes a tombstone.

On each node, an LSM tree:

  • Writes append to a write-ahead log (durability) and go into an in-memory memtable.
  • When the memtable reaches ~64 MB it is flushed as an immutable sorted SSTable.
  • Background compaction merges SSTables, drops overwritten values and expired tombstones.
  • Each SSTable has a Bloom filter, so a read skips files that cannot hold the key.

Cluster metadata: the ring (token → node), learned by gossip.

steps.title: High-level design
steps.ask: Draw the cluster and walk a write and a read.
steps.model:
Nodes sit on a consistent-hash ring; each owns many virtual nodes (e.g. 256) so load spreads evenly and a new node takes small slices from everyone.

Write:

  1. Client sends to any node; it becomes the coordinator.
  2. Hash the key; walk the ring clockwise to find the first 3 distinct physical nodes in different zones: the preference list.
  3. Send the write to all 3; reply success after W = 2 acks.

Read: ask the replicas, return after R = 2 replies, pick the newest version. If a replica was stale, send it the newer value (read repair).

With N = 3, R + W = 4 > N, so every read set overlaps the latest write set.

steps.title: Deep dive
steps.ask: Go deep on failures and conflicts.
steps.model:
Failure detection. Nodes gossip heartbeats every second; a node not heard from for several seconds is marked down locally. No central master.

Hinted handoff. If a replica is down, the coordinator writes to the next healthy node with a hint ("this belongs to C"). When C returns, the hint is replayed. Writes keep succeeding: that is the availability promise. It is a sloppy quorum, so until hints replay, R + W > N no longer guarantees a fresh read.

Anti-entropy. Replicas compare Merkle trees of their key ranges and sync only differing branches, so a node that missed hours of writes catches up without a full copy.

Conflicts. During a split two clients may write the same key on different sides. Last-write-wins by timestamp is simple but silently drops one write and trusts clocks. Vector clocks detect concurrent writes and return both siblings so the application merges them (e.g. union a shopping cart). Use LWW where a lost write is harmless (caches, last-seen times); use vector clocks or CRDTs where it is not (counters, carts).

steps.title: Bottlenecks & trade-offs
steps.ask: Bottlenecks and trade-offs.
steps.model:
• Hot keys: one key on 3 nodes can overload them. Cache it client-side or split it (key#1..key#10) for counters.
  • Compaction: steals disk bandwidth and causes latency spikes; throttle it and leave disk headroom.
  • Tombstones: deletes are writes; too many slow reads. Purge after a grace period longer than the longest node outage, or deleted data can come back.
  • Rebalancing after adding a node: stream data in the background, throttled.
  • Quorum tuning: R = 1, W = 1 is fastest but can read stale data; R = W = 2 balances; W = 3 is strongest but fails writes when any replica is down.
  • Leaderless vs leader-based: leaderless (Dynamo) stays writable during failures; leader per shard (Raft) gives linearizable reads but stalls during elections.

rubric: States a CAP position and offers tunable consistency.
Partitions with consistent hashing and virtual nodes.
Replicates to N nodes across zones and explains R + W > N.
Describes a storage engine (WAL, memtable, SSTables, compaction, Bloom filters).
Handles temporary failures with hinted handoff.
Repairs divergence with read repair and Merkle-tree anti-entropy.
Compares conflict resolution: last-write-wins versus vector clocks.
Sizes the cluster from data size and traffic.

title: Design a payment system
