evidence: A widely used industry system design question; no source ties it to GovTech or OGP, so practise it for the patterns it teaches (idempotency, double-entry ledgers, reconciliation).
prompt: "Design the payment backend for an online shop. Customers pay by card at checkout through an external payment processor. We must never charge twice and never lose track of money."

clarify.a: 10M payments a day, with 10× spikes during sales.

clarify.q: Do we handle card numbers ourselves?
clarify.a: No. Use the processor's hosted fields so we only see tokens.
Refunds yes. Seller payouts briefly.
Several, but no conversion inside a payment.

clarify.q: What is worse: a slow payment or a wrong one?
clarify.a: A wrong one. Correctness first.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.ask: Requirements. Say which properties are non-negotiable.
steps.model:
• Functional: create a payment for an order; authorise and capture through a processor; handle the processor's asynchronous results (webhooks); refund fully or partly; show payment status; daily reconciliation with the processor's settlement report.
  • Non-negotiable: never charge twice for one order, even with retries and timeouts; every cent accounted for in an immutable ledger; strong consistency for money state; full audit trail.
  • Non-functional: checkout p99 within a few seconds (processor-bound); highly available, but prefer refusing a payment to recording it wrongly; stay out of card-data compliance scope by never touching raw card numbers.
  • Out of scope: fraud models, currency conversion, tax.

steps.title: Estimates
steps.ask: Estimate payment rate, ledger growth and processor calls.
steps.model:
• 10M/day ÷ 86,400 = ~115 payments/s; sale peak ×10 = ~1.2k/s.
  • Each payment makes 2-4 ledger entries (authorise, capture, fees): ~30M entries/day × ~200 B = ~6 GB/day, ~2 TB/year. Fine for a relational database with partitioning by month.
  • Processor calls take ~1-3 s. At 1.2k/s that is ~3,600 requests in flight: use async I/O and connection pools, not a thread per request.
  • Webhooks arrive at about the payment rate, ~1k/s peak.

Conclusion: volume is moderate. The design is about correctness under retries, timeouts and partial failure.

steps.title: API & data model
steps.ask: API and data model.
steps.model:
• POST /payments {orderId, amountMinor, currency, paymentMethodToken} + Idempotency-Key → 201 {paymentId, status}. Same key returns the same result.
  • GET /payments/{id}
  • POST /payments/{id}/refunds {amountMinor} + Idempotency-Key
  • POST /webhooks/processor: signature verified.

Data (Postgres, synchronous replica):

  • payments(id, order_id UNIQUE, amount_minor BIGINT, currency, status, processor_ref, version). Status machine: CREATED → AUTHORISED → CAPTURED → SETTLED, or FAILED, or REFUNDED, plus PENDING_UNKNOWN while a processor result is unknown.
  • idempotency_keys(key PK, request_hash, response, created_at)
  • ledger_entries(id, txn_id, account_id, direction, amount_minor, created_at): append-only; each txn's debits equal its credits.
  • outbox(id, event, payload, published_at)

steps.title: High-level design
steps.ask: Draw it and walk one card payment.
steps.model:
1. Checkout page loads the processor's hosted card fields; the card number goes straight to the processor, which returns a token.
  2. The shop calls POST /payments with the token and an idempotency key derived from the order.
  3. The payment service inserts the idempotency row and a CREATED payment in one transaction. A duplicate key returns the stored response.
  4. It calls the processor to authorise and capture, passing the same idempotency key so the processor also deduplicates.
  5. On success it updates the payment to CAPTURED, writes balanced ledger entries and an outbox event in one transaction.
  6. An outbox relay publishes "payment captured" to the order service.
  7. Webhooks confirm or correct the final state; a nightly reconciliation job matches the processor's settlement file against the ledger.

steps.title: Deep dive
steps.ask: Go deep on timeouts and idempotency: the processor call timed out. Was the customer charged?
steps.model:
A timeout means unknown, not failed. Never retry with a new key: that is how customers get charged twice.

  • Mark the payment PENDING_UNKNOWN.
  • Retry with the same idempotency key; the processor returns the original result if the first call went through.
  • Or query the processor by your reference. A background job sweeps unknown payments every minute until resolved.
  • Webhooks are the processor's own answer; handle them idempotently (store processed event IDs) because they can arrive twice or out of order.

State transitions use optimistic locking: UPDATE payments SET status = 'CAPTURED', version = version + 1 WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2, so a late webhook cannot move a refunded payment back to captured.

Ledger: amounts are integers in minor units (no floats); entries are never edited; a correction is a new reversing entry.

steps.title: Bottlenecks & trade-offs
steps.ask: Bottlenecks and trade-offs.
steps.model:
• Processor outage: route to a second processor for new payments; never fail over a payment that is in an unknown state, or you may double-charge.
  • Hot ledger accounts: the shop's own revenue account is touched by every payment. Derive balances from entries asynchronously, or split into sub-accounts and sum.
  • Database: one primary with a synchronous replica; consistency over availability for money. Shard by merchant only when one primary is not enough.
  • Dual writes: writing the database and then publishing to a queue can lose events; the outbox pattern makes both one transaction.
  • Reconciliation catches what everything else misses: missing webhooks, processor bugs, fees. Treat mismatches as alerts, not logs.

rubric: Uses idempotency keys end to end, including on the processor call.
Treats a timeout as unknown and resolves it by retrying with the same key or querying.
Models payment status as a state machine with guarded transitions.
Keeps a double-entry, append-only ledger with integer minor units.
Avoids handling raw card data (tokens or hosted fields).
Uses an outbox (or equivalent) so state changes and events are not lost.
Handles duplicate and out-of-order webhooks.
Includes reconciliation against the processor's settlement report.
Prefers consistency over availability for money and says why.
